takeaways.headline: No published SROI with a documented method exists for any Northern Ireland children's or family service.
takeaways.detail: We reviewed 14 economic studies and ran 26 further searches that found nothing. Northern Ireland has 5: a cost of late intervention, a cost-utility trial, two Audit Office reports, and one SROI ratio (YZone, Portadown) that appears only in a press release with no published method.

takeaways.headline: None of the 8 programmes examined has a post-2019 outcome evaluation that compares children who got the service with children who did not.
takeaways.detail: Without that comparison, what would have happened anyway cannot be measured, and that is the core of an SROI. The one comparison-group study found (the Early Intervention Support Service, 2018) found no robust effect; a Sure Start study using linked records is under way with no results yet.

takeaways.headline: Northern Ireland's Audit Office found that youth justice interventions cannot currently be shown to be value for money (2017), and that the Department of Education's ability to assess value for money for Sure Start and related programmes is limited (2026).
takeaways.detail: Youth justice (2017): "The Department and the Youth Justice Agency lack the capacity to identify and apportion costs to the full range of interventions. Consequently, they cannot adequately assess their cost-effectiveness and cannot currently demonstrate that the interventions to reduce reoffending by young people represent value for money." Sure Start and educational disadvantage (2026): "Financial information is not consistently integrated with outcome reporting, limiting the Department's ability to undertake value for money assessments that consider both programme costs and the results achieved."

takeaways.headline: Sure Start would pay back its cost if it kept about 95 children a year out of residential care: about 1 in every 374 children it registers.
takeaways.detail: This is the size of effect needed, not evidence that it happens. The same test for the Family Support Hubs: 8.6 child-years of residential care, or 875 statutory family support cases, against 8,124 families referred.

takeaways.headline: The one ratio the evidence allowed, for VOYPIC, runs from £0.02 to £1.48 per £1 — a measure of the evidence, not of the charity.
takeaways.detail: It values a single self-reported outcome (79 of 161 respondents (49%) said they have a better quality of life, 2023-24) and rests on three assumptions no one has measured: how big the change is, how many would have improved anyway, and how much is due to VOYPIC. Its other reported outcomes have no published value, and no saving to public services is claimed.

takeaways.headline: Studies elsewhere found returns above £1 for similar services, but none is from Northern Ireland and they should not be transferred.
takeaways.detail: England: Sure Start Children's Centres — £2.05 per £1 (societal benefits vs up-front cost). Republic of Ireland: Youth work sector — Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) of 2.22:1. England only: Youth work sector — 3.2x to 6.4x (central); "a minimum of 2.5x and a maximum of 7.8x". Programmes, populations and costs differ, and some were commissioned by the sector itself.

existing.title: A cluster randomised controlled trial and evaluation and cost-effectiveness analysis of the Roots of Empathy schools-based programme for improving social and emotional well-being outcomes among 8- to 9-year-olds in Northern Ireland
existing.author: Connolly P, Miller S, Kee F, Sloan S, Gildea A, McIntosh E, Boyer N, Bland M (Queen's University Belfast et al.)
existing.method: cost-utility analysis within a cluster RCT (independent academic economic evaluation); not SROI
existing.headlineVerbatim: The ICER was £9571 per QALY gained (95% CI –£87,776 to £106,676)
otherFiguresVerbatim: The incremental cost was £153 (95% CI £14 to £292), significantly higher for ROE ( p = 0.032).
The incremental QALY gain of 0.0160 (95% CI –0.0143 to 0.0462) was not statistically significant ( p = 0.300).
The study also found that ROE was likely to be cost-effective in line with national guidelines.
existing.period: time horizon 3.75 years (45 months); costs in 2014 GBP
outcomesValued: secondary: SDQ prosocial and total difficulties scores (ICER per unit)
existing.financialProxies: Public sector perspective; unit costs from PSSRU 2014 (GP £46, school nurse £63, social worker £41, educational psychologist £41, etc.) and NHS Reference Costs 2013/14 (A&E £72, psychiatrist £228)
existing.deadweight: not applicable - counterfactual is the randomised waiting-list control group
existing.dropOff: discounting at 1.5% (NICE public health rate); 3.5% as sensitivity analysis
existing.assurance: peer-reviewed NIHR journal; independent of programme provider
existing.notes: Threshold £20,000-30,000 per QALY. Probability cost-effective 83.1% at £20,000 (90.1% at £30,000) in base case per Table 29. QALY gain itself not significant.
